s: Today's episode is all about learning itself — how we study, how we remember, and how we stay curious for life.
I love this topic, because I meet so many adults who tell me they want to learn new things, but they think they are too old or too busy to start.
That is such a shame, because almost everyone has a philomath inside them.
A philomath is simply a person who loves learning, and curiosity never really disappears.
It just waits for the right moment.
That's a beautiful way to put it.
When I was a student, I don't think I was much of a philomath.
My scholastic life was mostly about passing exams, not about loving knowledge.
I did my homework, I got decent scholastic results, but I never read anything extra.
I was a complete philomath as a kid.
I read encyclopedias for fun, I watched documentaries every weekend, and my scholastic record was full of gold stars because I genuinely enjoyed it.
I wish someone had told me back then that scholastic success does not have to mean sitting in a library all day.
You can be a philomath in your kitchen, in your garden, or even on your commute.
And you know, speaking of ways to keep learning every day, there is an app I always recommend to my friends.

The Muse English app gives you fresh daily words with photos and pronunciation, this very podcast, shadowing stories you can repeat out loud, quick quizzes, full grammar lessons, and even a leaderboard and points to keep you motivated.
It is completely free to install, and it turns ten spare minutes into real progress.
Ten minutes a day really adds up when the lessons are this good.
Maya, did you ever have a teacher who changed the way you learn?
My history teacher in high school was wonderful.
Her lessons were never didactic in a boring way.
You know, didactic means intended to teach a moral lesson, and sometimes didactic stories can feel preachy.
But she made every didactic point through real stories about real people, so the moral of each story came alive naturally.
The best didactic moments do not feel didactic at all.
My math teacher was the opposite kind of influence.
He was a little pedantic, honestly.
Pedantic means overly focused on tiny details and rules.
If you wrote the solution correctly but skipped one step, he marked it wrong.
Everything had to be pedantic perfection, down to the last decimal.
That kind of pedantic teaching can really hurt a student's confidence.
But I bet you learned to be precise.
But there is a difference between being precise and being pedantic about things that do not matter.
A good teacher corrects the important mistakes and lets the small ones go.
Speaking of teachers, my grandmother was not a teacher, but she managed to inculcate some wonderful habits in me.
To inculcate means to fix an idea in someone's mind through repeated teaching.
Every morning she made me repeat English words before breakfast.
She believed that if you inculcate a routine early, it stays with you forever.
The things our parents and grandparents inculcate in us become part of who we are.
My father tried to inculcate discipline in my brother and me.
He had this saying: practice ten minutes a day, and he would repeat it so often that he really did inculcate that rhythm into our lives.
That is exactly what the Muse English app asks for, by the way.
Funny how that number keeps coming back.
Now, I have to tell you about my university days, because that is where I met the most difficult and the most rewarding part of learning: interpretation.
Well, in my literature class, we had to write an exegesis every single week.
An exegesis is a careful, critical interpretation of a text.
You take one poem or one passage, and you write an exegesis that explains every symbol, every word choice, every hidden meaning.
The first exegesis I wrote was terrible.
My professor said my exegesis was more summary than analysis.
But by the third month, something clicked.
Writing an exegesis taught me to read slowly, to ask why the author chose this word and not that one.
Every good exegesis is really a conversation with the text.
Did you ever think about going further, like graduate school?
I actually applied, and I was accepted, but I never went.
To matriculate means to formally enroll at a university, and I was so close to matriculating.
I had the letter, I had the scholarship, and then life happened.
Once you matriculate, you are committed.
After you matriculate, there is no more dreaming about it — you have to do the work.
I kept the acceptance letter for a year, thinking maybe I would still matriculate the following autumn.
In the end, I didn't, and I sometimes wonder what would have happened if I had.
My cousin did matriculate last year, at the age of forty-two.
She decided to matriculate in a nursing program, and she is now in her second year.
She told me that when you matriculate as an adult, you appreciate every lecture so much more.
It proves it is never too late to matriculate, to enroll, to begin again.
And that is the perfect moment to mention something I care about.

The Muse English app makes daily learning easy: new words with photos and pronunciation, this Muse English podcast, shadowing stories, quick quizzes, full grammar lessons, and a leaderboard with points to keep you going.
It is completely free to install, and it fits around your schedule.
Ten minutes a day, real English progress.
Before we move on, Maya, can I ask you something?
Do you think our idea of education has changed?
When we were kids, learning was almost entirely scholastic.
You went to school, you studied for tests, and that was it.
Today, a philomath does not need a classroom.
There are online courses, evening classes, language exchanges.
You can be a philomath from your living room, and nobody will grade you on it.
That freedom is wonderful, but it also means we have to inculcate discipline in ourselves.
No teacher is watching, so we have to inculcate the habit ourselves.
That is the hard part of being an adult philomath.
I signed up for an online painting course last year and quit after two weeks.
Nobody was there to inculcate any routine in me, so I just drifted away.
I have done the same with guitar.
Maybe what we need is not another course but a small daily ritual.
Something didactic in the gentlest sense — a little lesson that teaches without preaching.
Less didactic pressure, more playful curiosity.
The best teachers I know are never pedantic about attendance or deadlines.
They make you want to come back.
And they never make you feel silly for asking questions.
Now, Maya, we have talked about loving learning, about teachers, about interpretation and university.
What advice would you give to someone who wants to become a philomath as an adult?
First, I would say: stop thinking of scholastic learning as the only kind of learning.
Your scholastic years are just the beginning.
Read what interests you, not what you think you should read.
A true philomath follows curiosity, not a curriculum.
And I would add: be careful with didactic material.
A didactic book can be wonderful, but if every lesson feels didactic and heavy, you will stop reading.
Mix the serious with the fun.
And do not be pedantic with yourself.
I see learners who are so pedantic about every mistake that they stop speaking entirely.
Being pedantic about grammar will not make you fluent.
Let your family and friends inculcate good habits in you, and try to inculcate good habits in others.
Surround yourself with people who inculcate curiosity instead of fear.
And if you ever study literature, try writing your own exegesis of a short poem.
An exegesis does not have to be academic.
Even a personal exegesis, your own interpretation, will deepen the way you read.
Let me do a quick recap of our seven words today.
A philomath is a person who loves learning.
Scholastic relates to schools and studies, like scholastic achievement or your scholastic record.
Didactic means intended to teach a moral lesson.
Pedantic means overly focused on tiny details and strict rules.
To inculcate means to fix an idea in the mind through repeated teaching.
An exegesis is a careful, critical interpretation of a text.
And to matriculate means to formally enroll at a university.
Seven words, and every one of them is about the adventure of learning itself.
So whether you matriculate this year or simply read one page a day, keep that philomath spirit alive.
Thanks for listening to Muse English.
